newsitem.title: POLAND: Polish zloty may be hurt if foreigners dump bills.
newsitem.headline: Polish zloty may be hurt if foreigners dump bills.

text.p: The Polish central bank's plan to freeze the zloty devaluation factor is likely to curb foreign purchases of treasuries and put pressure on the zloty as it would cap the interest rate differential, analysts said.

On Thursday, the National Bank of Poland President Hanna Gronkiewicz-Waltz told Reuters the crawling peg by which the zloty is devalued monthly would not be cut from the current one percent until year-on-year inflation fell to 13 percent.
Such a target has been set for the end of next year, with the current year-on-year rate at 19.5 percent.
"A steady crawling peg may freeze foreign short-term speculation on Polish treasuries," said Krzysztof Kozuchowski, dealer at ING Bank in Warsaw.

Analysts said the zloty may soften against the basket of currencies in the mid-term as foreign players, who earlier bought Polish treasuries expecting a slow-down in the zloty devaluation in line with offical forecasts, could pull out. "Foreign investors may start selling bills from their Polish portfolios. This is not a moment for entering the market," said Piotr Korcz, dealer at Bank Handlowy SA.

Analysts said foreign investors, who bought an estimated $1.5 billion of Polish treasuries in early 1996 after the crawling peg was last cut from 1.2 percent per month in early January, have already sold most of their holdings.
With the crawling peg at one percent monthly, the average zloty holding yielding about 19.5 percent would loose 12.7 percent of value in hard currency terms in a year.

This, coupled with about six percent in the cost of funds, would cut its eventual return for a foreign investor to less than 200 basis points. A fall in inflation and the subsequent fall in nominal yields would sqeeze the profit further, analysts said.
The budget plan for 1996 originally assumed the average rate of the monthly zloty devaluation against a basket of five western currencies would be 0.9 percent monthly.
Analysts said that in the long-term deposits held in western currencies could become relatively more profitable than zloty deposits, prompting banks to increase currency exposure.
"Strong hard currencies amid falling inflation would translate to a natural trend of lengthening currency positions," a chief dealer at a foreign bank here said.
At 1130 GMT, the zloty eased to 1.80/1.75 percent from the centre of its trading band, from 1.87/1.80 percent at 0720 GMT and Wednesday's close.
